source: Getzels & Csikszentmihalyi (1976) The Creative Vision (via search summaries of MIT Press Reader)
finding: Founding study. Art students sketched a still life from a table of objects. Some chose and arranged quickly (problem solvers). Others handled and rearranged objects at length (problem finders). Independent expert judges rated the finders' drawings as more original.
numbers: 31 art students; 27 objects; 1 hour each; about half explored at length. Exact effect sizes not seen in any source opened.
limits: Secondary summaries only; the book was not opened. One art school (Chicago, 1960s). Exploration time was observed, not manipulated, so it could reflect trait, mood or skill.
agent_relevance: Supports a dedicated S1 step that explores and restates before committing. Weak on size: no effect size is available to calibrate how much it should cost.

source: Getzels & Csikszentmihalyi (1976) follow-up of the art students (reviews and popular accounts)
finding: Problem-finding orientation was reported to predict later standing as an artist. Intelligence was reported as not correlated with studio performance or later professional success. Accounts disagree on follow-up timing.
numbers: Follow-up reported as 6 years, or 5 and 18 years, or 7 and 11 years, by different secondary sources. One source says 27 of the original 31 were located. No correlations seen.
limits: Conflicting secondary dates; the Project MUSE page itself was only an access-check page. Treat all follow-up numbers as unverified until the book is read.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code any follow-up effect size. Intelligence not predicting success hints the framing habit is separate from raw ability, which fits scaffolding a model rather than scaling it.

source: Freeman (1994) Appendix: The Artists Project, in Finding the Muse
finding: Later account of the same project. Artists with a discovery orientation produced work experts judged better and gained most early recognition. But problem finding was not the whole story: gregarious people and those who could withstand art-world pressure also fared better within a few years.
numbers: Project began 1963 at Chicago; students of fine art, advertising art, industrial art and art education. No sample sizes or statistics on the page.
quote: Problem finding was not the whole story.
limits: Page text only (full chapter paywalled). Names a co-factor (sociability, pressure tolerance) that the original claim did not control.
agent_relevance: Framing alone does not guarantee success. In our agent, framing must feed a tested pipeline (S4, S7), not stand alone.

source: van de Kamp et al. (2021) The relationship of types of exploration activities with originality of visual arts designs
finding: Conceptual replication of Getzels in secondary school. Coded exploration steps in student portfolios (association, combination, abstraction) and judged originality of the resulting designs. More remote exploration went with more original designs.
numbers: 11 Grade 11 visual arts students; 196 portfolio events; 147 with images rated by comparative judgment (scale separation reliability .85). All three exploration types together explained 31% of event-level variance in originality; combination alone about 5%, abstraction alone about 5%.
limits: Small N (11 students). Correlational, not manipulated. Coding agreement for raters 2 and 3 only moderate (Spearman .54 to .88). Authors say low N limits power.
agent_relevance: Gives a graded measure: how far an exploration step is from the stimulus predicts originality. A code check on distance between restatements (embedding distance) could mimic this.

source: van de Kamp et al. (2021) variance partition
finding: Originality varied mostly between a student's own events, not between students. So exploration is a situational act, not just a trait of certain people.
numbers: Variance partition coefficient 0.89: 89% of originality variance was at portfolio-event level; student-level variance was not significant.
limits: Eleven students only; a student-level effect could be hidden by low power.
agent_relevance: Supports making exploration a per-problem operator the program triggers, not a persona or global style (G4: no persona voters).

source: Okuda, Runco & Berger (1991) Creativity and the finding and solving of real-world problems
finding: A real-world problem-finding task predicted creative accomplishments better than standard divergent-thinking tasks and a real-world problem-solving task, and added significantly in hierarchical regression.
numbers: 77 elementary school students; four tasks; criterion was a checklist of creative activities. Coefficients not shown on the page.
limits: Abstract page only. Child sample; self-reported activity checklist as criterion; single study.
agent_relevance: Finding problems may predict creative output beyond fluency. Argues against scoring our agent's S1 by counting ideas alone.

source: Reiter-Palmon, Mumford, O'Connor Boes & Runco (1997) Problem construction and creativity: ability, cue consistency, active processing
finding: Problem construction ability predicted solution quality and originality, and the effect depended on cues: high-ability people did best when cues in the problem were inconsistent.
numbers: 195 undergraduates; 6 real-life problems; active processing manipulated by instruction, cue consistency by problem information. Effect sizes not on the page.
limits: Abstract page only. Ability was measured by a separate construction task. The interaction means the benefit is largest when the input is messy.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: reframing pays most when information conflicts. Fits G1 (reframe only on a signal) and using disagreement among attempts as the trigger.

source: Reiter-Palmon & Murugavel (2018) The effect of problem construction on team process and creativity
finding: Experiment with student teams. Teams told to construct the problem first were only marginally more original, no better in quality, but had higher satisfaction and lower conflict. Three different construction instructions did not differ.
numbers: 65 teams (46 construction, 19 control). Originality F(1,63)=2.06, p=.078, partial eta2=.03. Quality F=0.27, p=.30. Between the three instruction variants: originality F(2,43)=0.56, p=.58. Process satisfaction p=.040 eta2=.05; task conflict p=.014 eta2=.08.
limits: The abstract says construction teams generated 'more original ideas' but the reported test is marginal; small control group (19). Authors call for replication.
agent_relevance: Effect on originality is small and unreliable; the wording of the reframing instruction did not matter. Do not expect a large gain from one reframing slot.

source: Abdulla Alabbasi, Reiter-Palmon, Sultan & Ayoub (2021) Which divergent thinking index is more associated with problem finding ability?
finding: Problem-generation (PF) scores tracked verbal divergent thinking strongly but figural divergent thinking weakly. Flexibility was the best verbal predictor.
numbers: 90 sixth graders. Verbal flexibility with PF r=.71 to .76; verbal fluency r=.68 to .71; verbal originality r=.55 to .61. Figural correlations with PF roughly .14 to .30. Verbal DT explained 40 to 58% of PF variance; figural 28 to 37%. 1% vs 3% originality cutoff did not change results.
limits: Verbal-verbal overlap may be shared method. Only problem discovery was scored. Instruction asked for different and novel problems, which may favour flexibility. Lines task dropped for low reliability.
agent_relevance: Producing many different categories of problem statement (flexibility), not just many, is the useful signal. Count distinct frame categories in code.

source: Abdulla Alabbasi et al. (2021) literature table of DT and PF studies
finding: Earlier studies of the link between divergent thinking and problem finding conflict. Some find positive links; some find positive links with PF quantity but negative with PF quality.
numbers: Examples in the table: N=395, fluency vs hypothesis-formulation r from .05 to .34; N=84 TTCT positive with PF quantity, negative with PF quality; N=80 PG test with other DT r from .31 to .51; one high-school study verbal originality r=.23, flexibility r=.18, no figural link.
limits: Table is the authors' selection; studies differ in tests, scoring and age. Not a systematic meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Quantity of problem statements and quality of them can move in opposite directions. Select among restatements by a check, not by volume (G5, G8).

source: Meta-analysis of the Problem Generation test (2024 OSF preprint) The reliability and validity of problem generation tests
finding: Meta-analysis of the Problem Generation (PG) test, the main paper-and-pencil measure of problem finding. Reliable, with moderate validity against other creativity measures.
numbers: 19 investigations out of 617 candidates. Reliability alpha=.816 (95% CI .786 to .842; k=43, N=2,029). Convergent validity r=.463 (CI .406 to .518; k=125, N=2,573). Correlation among fluency, flexibility and originality indices r=.590 (k=26, N=2,145). Data heterogeneous; moderators did not explain it.
limits: Read the record's abstract only (OSF API), not the full text. Preprint; r=.46 is moderate, so most variance in other creativity scores is unexplained.
agent_relevance: Problem finding is measurable and about as predictive as divergent thinking, not more. Keep S1 modest and cheap (G7).

source: Claim in Abdulla Alabbasi et al. (2021) citing earlier meta-analyses on PF
finding: The authors state a recent meta-analysis found a significant positive PF to creativity correlation, similar in size to the divergent thinking to creative achievement correlation, and that PF was the strongest predictor and PF training the most effective. The meta-analysis itself is not named in the text I read.
numbers: No effect sizes in the passage.
limits: Second-hand claim with unnamed source; unverified.
agent_relevance: Treat 'PF is the greatest predictor' as unconfirmed until the primary meta-analysis is found.

source: Linnell & Reiter-Palmon (2026) Cognitive underpinnings of malevolent creativity: the role of problem construction
finding: People who restated an ambiguous workplace problem in more distinct ways later produced more original ideas, and also more harmful ideas. Reframing amplifies both.
numbers: 155 working adults on Prolific; hierarchical regression after age, impression management and problem-solving experience. Problem construction fluency predicted originality beta=.41 (p<.001), harmfulness beta=.29 (p<.001), malevolent creativity beta=.26 (p=.001).
limits: Correlational; people already intent on harm might write more harm-oriented restatements. Low base rate of harmful ideas; vignette had no explicit target.
agent_relevance: A reframing slot widens the whole idea space, including bad directions. Pair it with a check and a safety filter before selection (G3, G8).

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero & Oulasvirta (2025) No evidence for LLMs being useful in problem reframing
finding: Large between-subjects test of GPT-4o as a reframing aid for design problems. No condition (manual, direct, free-form, or structured Dorst 9-step) differed on expert-rated novelty or usefulness.
numbers: N=280 after exclusions (456 recruited); 4 conditions; 3 design problems; 15 expert raters scored 280 frames; all p>.05 for novelty/usefulness and agency. Perceived helpfulness CSI: direct 64.28, structured 64.85, free-form 61.01.
quote: No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing
limits: Only GPT-4o; crowd workers, not professional designers; the instruction to submit best-quality frames may shape behaviour. Single-shot frames, no iteration. I read the first 100,000 of 138,647 characters.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that adding an LLM reframer does not by default raise frame novelty. S1 and O8 need a measured gain before they are kept (G7).

source: Shin et al. (2025) expertise moderator
finding: Expertise moderated the result: experts using LLMs wrote more novel frames than novices did, so the LLM widened the gap rather than closing it.
numbers: Experts produced 12.54% more novel frames in LLM conditions (Z=2.70, p=.01). Free-form gap 20.84% was not significant (p=.06). Structured condition: experts reported 15.69% more agency (p=.02). Of 218 LLM-condition participants, 93 reported problems; 31 said frames were not novel, 14 repetitive, 12 not useful.
limits: Expert/novice split by a 5-item quiz (3 or more correct = expert). Several subgroup tests; usefulness and ownership showed no expert gap.
agent_relevance: A reframer helps only when the reader can judge frames. Our program must supply the judge (a check), since the model cannot.

source: Sood, Wan, Paris & Grace (2026) What makes LLM-generated answers valuable for research problem reframing?
finding: Small user study. A structured 'Dorst frame' prompt was picked as interesting more often than direct answers or all-content answers, but tastes differed by person.
numbers: 7 research students; 27 LLM answers each from 3 prompt strategies. Interesting: dorst frame 29/189, direct 17/189, all-content 17/189. Top-3 picks: dorst 11 of 21 (52%), direct 7 (33%), all-content 3 (14%). 5 of 7 said top answers made them rethink their question.
limits: N=7, self-report, no measure of later research change, no novelty control. Authors note LLM frames still lack the novelty needed as foundations.
agent_relevance: Mild support for a frame-style prompt, but interest is not outcome. Keep it behind a check rather than a human taste signal.

source: Su et al. (2026) Knowing but not showing: LLMs recognize ambiguity but rarely ask clarifying questions
finding: Models can often label a question ambiguous when asked, but in normal answering they almost never ask for clarification. Adding retrieved context makes them ask even less.
numbers: 10 models (6 OpenAI, 2 Claude, 2 Qwen). Answer rate typically above 95%; 80 to 95% of responses were pure answers. Claude family asked most, up to about 5% on ambiguous questions without context. Accuracy on ambiguous questions 10 to 15 points lower for strong models. GPT-4 recognised only 15 to 27% of ambiguous questions in the judgement task while about 90% right on unambiguous ones. Context lifted unambiguous accuracy 54% to 67%, ambiguous 46% to 55%.
limits: Behaviour labelled by an LLM judge (gpt-5-nano, gpt-5); gold ambiguity labels from a benchmark; no fix tested.
agent_relevance: Models do not find problems unprompted. S1 must force a code-run step (list assumptions, flag ambiguity) because the model will not do it by itself.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: Blind expert review found LLM-generated research ideas more novel than ideas by expert humans, with slightly lower feasibility.
numbers: 79 reviewers, 298 reviews, 49 ideas per condition. Novelty per idea: Human 4.86 (SD 1.26), AI 5.62 (p=.03), AI plus human rerank 5.78 (p<.01). Feasibility per review: human 6.61, AI 6.34, rerank 6.44, not significant. Overall score: only rerank beat human (p=.04).
limits: Topics were assigned, ideas style-normalised. Novelty judged on proposals, not outcomes.
agent_relevance: Even with the problem given, LLMs can match humans on novelty; what is missing is problem selection, which these experts did not do.

source: Si et al. (2024) diversity and judge limits
finding: Scaling LLM idea generation hits a wall: most new ideas repeat earlier ones. LLM judges ranked ideas near chance.
numbers: Of 4,000 generated seed ideas only about 200 were non-duplicate (cosine similarity threshold 0.8), roughly 5%; accumulated unique ideas plateau. Best LLM judge accuracy 53.3% vs human inter-reviewer 56.1%; GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%; GPT-4o direct 50.0%.
limits: Duplicate threshold set by manual inspection. Benchmark is the authors' own top/bottom 25% of reviews.
agent_relevance: Repeated reframing from one model will collapse onto few frames. Count distinct frames in code and stop when new ones stop appearing (G1, G12). Supports G8.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a step back: evoking reasoning via abstraction in LLMs
finding: Asking a model first to state the general principle behind a question, then answering, raised accuracy on science and knowledge tasks.
numbers: PaLM-2L: MMLU Physics 66.4 to 73.2; Chemistry 70.9 to 81.8; TimeQA 41.5 to 68.7 (with retrieval); TimeQA hard 40.4 to 62.3 vs GPT-4 42.6; MuSiQue 35.5 to 42.6. GPT-4 MMLU Physics 69.4 to 84.5. Llama2-70B Physics 51.9 to 64.8.
limits: Graded by PaLM-2L as judge (authors report 97 to 99% agreement with humans). Different TimeQA gain numbers appear across versions (27 vs 34 points).
agent_relevance: Closest tested analogue of an O8 reframe: restate at a higher level before solving. Positive when the task has first-principles structure.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Step-back error analysis and null results
finding: Step-back fixed errors but also introduced new ones, and the remaining errors are mostly in reasoning, not in the abstraction step. No gain on GSM8K.
numbers: MMLU Physics: corrected 20.5% of baseline errors, introduced 11.9% new; over 90% of remaining errors in reasoning. TimeQA: fixed 39.9%, broke 5.6%. StrategyQA: fixed 15.4%, broke 6.1%. GSM8K: step-back 84.3 vs 1-shot 84.5 vs zero-shot CoT 84.4.
limits: The authors note abstraction is not needed for simple facts or questions already at first principles.
agent_relevance: Reframe only when a signal says the direct frame is not enough (G1). Net gain is positive but includes damage; keep the original attempt to compare in code.

source: Deng, Zhang, Chen & Gu (2023) Rephrase and Respond: let LLMs ask better questions for themselves
finding: Having the model rewrite the question before answering lifted GPT-4 accuracy on ten tasks, with big gains where the question was badly worded.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot average 64.95 to 89.77 with RaR over ten tasks. Examples: Last letter concat (4 words) 21.36 to 86.82; Last letter (2) 52.05 to 99.09; Day-even 54.29 to 93.33; Dates 69.92 to 75.88; CSQA 84.09 to 85.45 (little gain when the question is already clear).
limits: Tasks mostly synthetic or ambiguous by design. GPT-4 only in the main table. Gains shrink when questions are well formed.
agent_relevance: Rewriting helps when the input is poorly framed; use ambiguity or low agreement as the trigger. Gains on clear questions are small.

source: Deng et al. (2023) RaR across models and with chain of thought
finding: Rewrites by a stronger model help a weaker one; stronger models gain more from rewriting. Rephrasing can repair flawed worked examples in chain of thought.
numbers: Vicuna-13b accuracy with its own rewrites vs GPT-4 rewrites: Even-day 58.10 vs 61.90; CSQA 51.36 vs 55.00; Sports 65.00 vs 73.64; Last letter (2) 5.45 vs 10.45. Four-shot chain of thought with flawed examples fell to 52.27% on four-word last-letter concatenation.
limits: Only GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna tested; the chain-of-thought result uses deliberately corrupted examples.
agent_relevance: Reframe quality depends on the reframing model. A small model may reframe worse than it solves, so test the reframer separately (G7).

source: AINSTEIN (2025) Assessing LLMs' ability to solve AI research problems from problem statements
finding: LLM agents given only a problem statement extracted from a paper often produce a viable solution but rarely the published one; they fail on cross-domain analogy.
numbers: Success over 70% of problems; strict rediscovery of the published solution under 19%; blind study with 20 domain experts validated metrics; scaled to 1,214 ICLR 2025 papers with an LLM judge.
limits: Abstract page only (model names not read). LLM-as-judge at scale; problem statements given, not discovered.
agent_relevance: Again the problem is given, not found. Failure on cross-domain transfer marks the limit of text-only reframing.

source: Status of direct replication of the Getzels still-life experiment (this session's sources)
finding: No direct replication of the 1960s still-life experiment was found. Later work consists of conceptual replications in other age groups or tasks (van de Kamp 2021, Okuda 1991) and correlational tests of problem-finding measures.
numbers: Not applicable: absence of a located direct replication; no failed replication seen either.
limits: Absence from a limited search (web search quota ran out); not proof that none exists. Original numbers remain unverified.
agent_relevance: The claim 'explore first, then pick' rests on moderate, mostly correlational support. Label it [S] in the schema, not [E].

source: Reiter-Palmon et al. (1997) boundary condition summary
finding: Cue consistency moderates problem construction: benefit appears when cues are diverse or inconsistent. With consistent cues there is little to reconcile.
numbers: Same study as b07: 195 undergraduates, 6 problems.
limits: Abstract-level. The interaction size is not on the page.
agent_relevance: Trigger reframing on conflicting evidence (attempts disagree), matching G1 and S6 impasse routing.
